verses.text: Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to Yahweh, and said, “I will sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously. The horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.
Yah is my strength and song. He has become my salvation. This is my God, and I will praise him; my father’s God, and I will exalt him.
Yahweh is a man of war. Yahweh is his name.
He has cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea. His chosen captains are sunk in the Red Sea.
The deeps cover them. They went down into the depths like a stone.
Your right hand, Yahweh, is glorious in power. Your right hand, Yahweh, dashes the enemy in pieces.
In the greatness of your excellency, you overthrow those who rise up against you. You send out your wrath. It consumes them as stubble.
With the blast of your nostrils, the waters were piled up. The floods stood upright as a heap. The deeps were congealed in the heart of the sea.
The enemy said, ‘I will pursue. I will overtake. I will divide the plunder. My desire shall be satisfied on them. I will draw my sword, my hand shall destroy them.’
You blew with your wind. The sea covered them. They sank like lead in the mighty waters.
Who is like you, Yahweh, among the gods? Who is like you, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?
You stretched out your right hand. The earth swallowed them.
“You, in your loving kindness, have led the people that you have redeemed. You have guided them in your strength to your holy habitation.
The peoples have heard. They tremble. Pangs have taken hold on the inhabitants of Philistia.
Then the chiefs of Edom were dismayed. Trembling takes hold of the mighty men of Moab. All the inhabitants of Canaan have melted away.
Terror and dread falls on them. By the greatness of your arm they are as still as a stone — until your people pass over, Yahweh, until the people pass over who you have purchased.
You shall bring them in, and plant them in the mountain of your inheritance, the place, Yahweh, which you have made for yourself to dwell in; the sanctuary, Lord, which your hands have established.
Yahweh shall reign forever and ever.”

For the horses of Pharaoh went in with his chariots and with his horsemen into the sea, and Yahweh brought back the waters of the sea on them; but the children of Israel walked on dry land in the middle of the sea.
Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand; and all the women went out after her with tambourines and with dances.
Miriam answered them, “Sing to Yahweh, for he has triumphed gloriously. The horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea.”
Moses led Israel onward from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur; and they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water.
When they came to Marah, they couldn’t drink from the waters of Marah, for they were bitter. Therefore its name was called Marah.
The people murmured against Moses, saying, “What shall we drink?”
Then he cried to Yahweh. Yahweh showed him a tree, and he threw it into the waters, and the waters were made sweet. There he made a statute and an ordinance for them, and there he tested them;

and he said, “If you will diligently listen to Yahweh your God’s voice, and will do that which is right in his eyes, and will pay attention to his commandments, and keep all his statutes, I will put none of the diseases on you, which I have put on the Egyptians; for I am Yahweh who heals you.”
They came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water, and seventy palm trees: and they encamped there by the waters.

footnotes.content: Here's where faith finds its voice. Moses and all Israel break into song—not after a quiet moment of reflection, but right there at the sea's edge, waters still settling. When you've tasted deliverance this fresh, your first instinct is to *sing* it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Notice how quickly the personal claim follows the victory: *my* strength, *my* salvation, *my* God. It's not borrowed confidence or secondhand faith. The Lord invites each of us to make His triumph our own, to feel His deliverance in our bones.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh is a man of war—a startling claim when we're used to thinking of strength as gentle. But here, His warfare *defends* the helpless. This is what divine strength looks like when it stands against tyranny.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's finest—the chariots, the army, his chosen captains—swallowed by the sea. The powers that threatened to crush God's people vanish in a moment. This is what happens when you oppose the God who made the seas.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Down like a stone—final, swift, total. The Psalms will echo this image, but here it's immediate truth: what seemed unstoppable is now unreachable, beneath the weight of the waters. God's judgment runs deeper than our fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God's right hand becomes the measure of all power and all compassion. The same hand that dashes enemies is the one that will lead Israel through the wilderness, gather them, feed them. Strength and grace are not opposites here—they're the same hand, turned toward His people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His wrath consumes like fire consumes straw—unstoppable, complete, nothing left. But notice: it falls only on those who rise up against Him. This is judgment, not caprice. God's anger is always the anger of one who has been resisted, not one who seeks to hurt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The image of waters piled up like a heap—this is how Exodus remembers what happened at the sea. The same waters that drowned the chariots had stood upright, hard as a wall, so Israel could walk through on dry ground. One act of divine power, two opposite effects.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Listen to Pharaoh's boast—'I will pursue, I will overtake, I will divide the plunder.' He spoke with certainty, with the voice of a conqueror. But God has already heard these words. They're answered before they're finished.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Your wind, Lord. One breath. Not a battle, not a contest—just the Lord's breath, and the sea covers them, and they sink like lead. This is how easily the Lord disposes of what terrified His people only hours before.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Who is like You? It's the only honest question left after what they've seen. Not 'What do we do now?' or 'Where do we go?' but 'Who else could be like this?'—and the answer echoes across the centuries. None. Only the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The earth swallowed them—as if creation itself rises to swallow God's enemies. Nature bends to His will. There's a mercy even in this: the sea doesn't need to hold them; the earth completes what God's hand began.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the song turns from judgment to love. Loving-kindness led them. They were redeemed, and now guided to the holy place. This is the heart of it all—not just that God defeats enemies, but that He gathers His people close and leads them home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Philistia heard, and trembled. News travels—the report of the sea crossed borders. What happened to Pharaoh's army became a sign to all the nations that this God cannot be resisted. Sometimes our deliverance witnesses beyond what we see.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Edom, Moab, Canaan—the nations around tremble and melt away. They hear the name of the Lord attached to Israel's rescue, and power drains from their limbs. This is the reputation the Lord earned on Israel's behalf that day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Terror and dread fall upon them, but Israel passes through safely. One people frozen in fear, another moving forward under the Lord's protection. The same act of power divides humanity into those who oppose God and those who belong to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The mountain of His inheritance—this is the land He has prepared, and later, Mount Zion where His house will stand. The song looks forward now, from the sea toward the sanctuary. Deliverance is never only rescue; it's always movement toward home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh shall reign forever and ever. The song ends not with Israel's safety or the fading threat, but with the eternal kingship of God. This is what the victory means: not just that we're saved today, but that the King who saved us will never cease to reign.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Now the narrative voice recounts what was sung—the horses, the chariots, the horsemen, the waters returning. This is the plain-spoken testimony that backs up the triumph. What felt impossible happened exactly as the Lord declared it would.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Miriam the prophetess—she speaks for God. She takes up the tambourine and leads the women in celebration. Notice that the Lord gave her a voice and a role; she steps into it without hesitation. Deliverance invites the whole people into praise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Miriam and the women sing the refrain, repeating the triumph: 'He has thrown the horse and rider into the sea.' Corporate worship born in the moment—every voice joining, every tambourine sounding. The song travels through the camp, and joy becomes infectious.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses led Israel onward from the Red Sea into the wilderness of Shur—the same wilderness where Hagar once fled. The victory song still echoing, but now they march into dry, hard country where water cannot be found. Joy and testing often travel together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They come to Marah—and its waters are bitter. The name itself means 'bitter.' After the sea's mighty power, they find a place where even the water rebels against them. Nature itself seems to test whether their new faith will hold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The people murmur against Moses. Three days without water—thirst does terrible things to hope. They sang at the sea; now they complain in the wilderness. The shadow between memory and present trouble is exactly where faith lives or dies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses cried to the Lord, not to the people. He brings the complaint to God, and God showed him a tree—a simple thing, thrown into the waters, and they became sweet. This is God's answer to bitterness: transformation through obedience and faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord makes a statute here—listen and obey, do what is right, keep His commandments, and He will protect them from the diseases that afflicted Egypt. It's a covenant offer: if you stay close to Me, I will be your healer. The wilderness becomes a classroom where obedience is taught.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elim—twelve springs of water, seventy palm trees. After Marah's bitterness, abundance. Readers today hear an echo here: the Lord doesn't leave us in testing forever. There is always an Elim waiting, a place of plenty that teaches us He cares for the journey itself, not just the destination.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
